PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 89 — Lesson 113: Skin & Soft-Tissue Infections

FNP-level goal: Distinguish cellulitis, abscess, wound infection, and dangerous deep infection from common mimics; determine when source control, targeted testing, outpatient antibiotics, admission, or urgent surgery is needed; and use antimicrobial stewardship without missing limb- or life-threatening disease.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate nonpurulent cellulitis, erysipelas, abscess, purulent wound infection, and common noninfectious mimics.
  • Explain why a drainable collection requires a source-control decision rather than antibiotics alone.
  • Perform a focused skin and systemic assessment that identifies severity, host risk, portal of entry, vascular status, and deep-tissue red flags.
  • Select diagnostic tests and antimicrobial therapy based on clinical question, severity, epidemiology, allergy, renal function, interactions, pregnancy, and local guidance.
  • Recognize necrotizing infection, septic physiology, orbital or facial danger areas, rapidly progressive infection, and immunocompromised hosts as urgent escalation problems.

Part 1 — Define the Syndrome Before Choosing an Antibiotic

Skin and soft-tissue infection is not a single diagnosis. Nonpurulent cellulitis is a spreading infection of skin and subcutaneous tissue, often warm, tender, edematous, and ill-defined. Erysipelas is more superficial and may have a more sharply demarcated elevated border. An abscess is a collection of purulent material and may be fluctuant, point, drain, or show a focal pocket on ultrasound. An infected wound has a portal, tissue injury, and potentially foreign material or deeper involvement. The correct plan follows the syndrome, not just the presence of redness.

Start by asking what happened first: a break in skin, shaving, bite, injection, trauma, edema, ulcer, surgery, prior abscess, water exposure, animal exposure, or rapidly enlarging pain. Ask about fever, chills, malaise, diabetes, peripheral arterial disease, immunosuppression, venous disease, lymphedema, pregnancy, recent antimicrobials, allergies, renal disease, anticoagulants, and prior resistant organisms. Time course and host factors affect both differential and disposition.

Part 2 — Cellulitis Has Many Mimics

Unilateral warmth, tenderness, expanding erythema, and edema can support cellulitis, but bilateral lower-leg redness, chronic hyperpigmentation, itch, scaling, or longstanding edema often points toward venous stasis dermatitis or other inflammatory conditions. Contact dermatitis may be sharply patterned around an exposure and more pruritic than tender. Gout can create an acutely inflamed joint. Deep venous thrombosis may cause unilateral swelling and pain. Herpes zoster, inflammatory arthritis, lymphedema, hematoma, and superficial thrombophlebitis may also enter the differential.

Do not use normal temperature or absence of leukocytosis to exclude infection in a high-risk patient, and do not use any one laboratory value to prove cellulitis. The diagnosis is clinical. When the examination is equivocal, targeted imaging, laboratory studies, or close reassessment may be more useful than an automatic antibiotic prescription.

Part 3 — Source Control Is a Clinical Decision

Antibiotics penetrate poorly into some walled-off purulent collections. A fluctuant abscess, focal tenderness with spontaneous drainage, or ultrasound-confirmed collection should prompt consideration of incision and drainage by a clinician trained and equipped to perform it, or referral to a setting that can. Culture of purulent material may be useful in selected recurrent, severe, unusual, treatment-failure, or high-risk cases and should answer a management question. Do not swab intact cellulitic skin and mistake surface organisms for the cause of deep infection.

After source control, reassess the need for adjunctive antibiotics based on systemic features, surrounding cellulitis, host risks, depth, size, anatomy, recurrence, and local practice guidance. The FNP should not assume drainage alone is always enough, nor that antibiotics alone are a substitute for drainage when a collection is present.

Part 4 — Focused Examination and Severity Assessment

Measure vital signs and appearance first. Inspect color, warmth, tenderness, edema, induration, fluctuance, drainage, bullae, necrosis, crepitus, lymphangitic streaking, distal perfusion, sensation, range of motion, pain with passive movement, and proximity to joints, tendons, eyes, hands, genitals, or perineum. Marking a boundary can support trend assessment when clinically appropriate, but a marker line never substitutes for a reassessment plan. Examine likely portals of entry such as toe-web maceration, fissures, ulcers, wounds, injections, eczema, or trauma.

Document location, dimensions, photographs when consented and secure, systemic findings, host risk, differential, and disposition. In a diabetic foot, hand infection, facial infection, animal bite, surgical wound, or immunocompromised patient, an apparently small lesion may carry substantially higher risk. Ask whether the patient can obtain medication, perform wound care, return quickly, and recognize worsening; outpatient treatment is a plan, not merely a prescription.

Part 5 — Deep and Necrotizing Infection: Do Not Miss the Clock

Severe pain out of proportion, rapidly progressive swelling or erythema, bullae, skin anesthesia, dusky or necrotic skin, crepitus, systemic toxicity, hypotension, confusion, metabolic deterioration, or failure to improve as expected should raise concern for necrotizing or deep soft-tissue infection. The absence of one classic finding does not make the situation safe. Suspected necrotizing infection requires immediate emergency and surgical evaluation; do not delay definitive care while waiting for a reassuring laboratory score or a nonessential outpatient test.

Deep-space infection, flexor tendon involvement, septic joint, orbital cellulitis, perineal infection, facial infection with eye symptoms, and hand infections have anatomic consequences that lower the threshold for emergency or specialty evaluation. The location matters as much as the size.

Part 6 — Diagnostics and Stewardship

Order tests because their result will change management. Ultrasound can help distinguish abscess from cellulitis when examination is unclear. Plain radiographs may help identify foreign body, gas, fracture, or bony concerns in selected wounds. Advanced imaging, blood cultures, inflammatory markers, and specialist consultation are reserved for severity, depth, systemic illness, unusual pathogens, or diagnostic uncertainty. Culture a clinically meaningful specimen when it can guide therapy; routine cultures in uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis are often low yield.

Choose empiric antimicrobial coverage to match syndrome, severity, likely organisms, local resistance information, prior culture data, exposures, allergies, kidney function, pregnancy, interactions, and patient access. Then narrow or change therapy based on clinical response and microbiology. Avoid prolonged or repeated courses without reassessing the diagnosis, source control, adherence, and deeper complications. Stewardship means giving the right treatment at the right time—not withholding treatment from a genuinely infected patient.

Part 7 — Follow-Up Is Part of the Prescription

Give patients clear instructions about expected early response, medication use, wound care, hydration, elevation or edema care when appropriate, pain control, and exact return precautions. Reassessment interval depends on severity and host factors. Worsening pain, spreading erythema, fever, vomiting, new bullae, numbness, drainage, inability to bear weight or use a limb, confusion, or no expected improvement should trigger earlier review. Unreliable follow-up, barriers to medication, or inability to perform self-care may make outpatient management unsafe.

Part 8 — FNP Case: Warm Red Leg or Venous Stasis?

A patient with chronic bilateral edema has itchy scaly lower legs with longstanding brown discoloration and no fever, focal tenderness, or rapid spread. The FNP resists the reflex to prescribe antibiotics for bilateral redness, assesses venous and skin-care needs, and provides a documented reassessment plan. The important reasoning step is recognizing that chronic inflammatory signs can mimic infection.

Part 9 — FNP Case: The Fluctuant Forearm Mass

A patient presents with a painful fluctuant forearm mass with purulent drainage and surrounding redness. The FNP identifies a likely abscess, assesses systemic illness, neurovascular status, size, location, and injection or bite history, and arranges appropriate drainage capability rather than relying on oral antibiotics alone. The plan includes culture when clinically useful, wound follow-up, and return precautions.

Part 10 — FNP Case: Pain Out of Proportion

A patient with diabetes has rapidly worsening thigh pain, edema, fever, and a dusky blistering area after minor trauma. The degree of pain and systemic illness is inconsistent with uncomplicated cellulitis. The FNP activates emergency transfer for possible deep or necrotizing infection; delay for routine outpatient treatment could cost tissue and life.

FNP High-Yield Framework: SOFT

  1. S — Syndrome: cellulitis, abscess, wound infection, mimic, or deep infection?
  2. O — Obtain source control: identify a collection, drain or refer when indicated, and collect meaningful specimens selectively.
  3. F — Find severity and host risk: vitals, systemic illness, anatomy, diabetes, immunosuppression, vascular disease, and follow-up capacity.
  4. T — Track response: explicit reassessment, return precautions, medication safety, and diagnostic reconsideration if not improving.

Take-Home Summary

Safe SSTI care requires syndrome recognition, source control, assessment of severity and anatomy, targeted diagnostics, and stewardship-informed treatment. Redness alone is not cellulitis, an abscess is not just cellulitis with more antibiotics, and pain out of proportion or systemic toxicity is not an outpatient watch-and-wait problem. The FNP protects patients by building a plan that includes reassessment and escalation, not just a drug choice.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace emergency assessment, surgical or infectious-disease consultation, local antimicrobial guidance, procedure training, or individualized treatment. Rapid progression, severe pain, bullae, crepitus, necrosis, systemic toxicity, eye involvement, or concern for deep infection requires emergency evaluation.
